A.explanation: At the top only the unchanged horizontal component remains so speed is minimum but non-zero, and symmetry with no air resistance returns the speed to $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$ on landing.

B.explanation: The minimum speed is greater than zero, but without air resistance no extra energy is gained so the landing speed cannot exceed $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Speed is never zero because the horizontal component $20\cos45^{\circ}$ stays constant even when the vertical component is momentarily zero at the top.

D.explanation: Speed is never zero for an angled launch, and with negligible air resistance mechanical energy is conserved so the landing speed is not less than $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Recall that with negligible air resistance the horizontal velocity stays constant while the vertical velocity decreases to zero at the highest point then increases downward.
Think about speed as $\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ at the top, and use energy conservation or symmetry to compare the landing speed with the $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$ launch speed.
walkthrough: Resolve the initial $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $45^{\circ}$: $v_x = 20\cos45^{\circ}$ and $v_y = 20\sin45^{\circ}$, both about $14.1 \text{m s}^{-1}$.
With no air resistance, $v_x$ remains $14.1 \text{m s}^{-1}$ throughout the flight while gravity reduces $v_y$ to zero at the top and then increases it in the downward direction.
Speed is the magnitude $v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$, so at the top $v = \sqrt{14.1^2+0^2} \approx 14.1 \text{m s}^{-1}$, which is a minimum greater than zero.
On the way down $|v_y|$ grows again, so $v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ increases from that minimum.

By symmetry of projectile motion, or conservation of kinetic plus gravitational potential energy from the same ground level, the object returns with the same speed magnitude $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$ just before impact.
Decreasing to a non-zero minimum then increasing back to $20 \text{m s}^{-1}$ matches the description. This is option A.
